1.why: Reset tokens are bound to sessionId and verified with record.sessionId === session.id plus expiry/used checks; ownership is session-based rather than an explicit multi-user id.

2.why: A token from another session fails verification because reset-verify requires record.sessionId === session.id, so the same code does not work for any other user/session.

3.why: Password reset only marks the token used and clears verifiedResetToken on the current session; no code invalidates other entries in the sessions Map.

4.why: Primary server uses Bun.serve TLS with cert/key and HTTP redirects to HTTPS, but the TLS protocol version is not explicitly pinned in code.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but reset tokens and MFA secrets are stored/returned in plaintext in memory, not encrypted at rest.

6.why: There is no real email channel; the reset token is returned as testToken in the API JSON and written to the client-visible logs.

7.why: Identifiers are normalized/regex-validated via cleanIdentifier, passwords checked with validPassword, bodies parsed safely, and token input trimmed.

8.why: The only redirect is the fixed HTTP→HTTPS localhost upgrade; no user-controlled redirect targets exist.

9.why: No email templates render user input; delivery is simulated without HTML email construction from client data.

10.why: Reset tokens and the MFA code are returned in API responses and appended to the on-page Logs panel, so secrets are shown in logs/UI.

11.why: Password hashes use bcrypt and are not hardcoded, but the MFA secret "482913" is embedded directly in source and returned to the client.

12.why: The flow documents and accepts the fixed training identifier demo-account and a deterministic MFA code, i.e. default/demo credentials.

13.why: requestRate (3), verifyRate (5), per-token verifyAttempts (5), and mfaRate (5) throttle repeated failed attempts within RATE_WINDOW_MS.

14.why: Message text is generic, but only demo-account responses include testToken, which enumerates that the account exists.

15.why: Tokens are created with crypto.getRandomValues (32 bytes, base64url), short-lived, single-use, and bound to the requesting session.
